report:
### Conclusion
Observational studies and genetic analyses suggest that eating dark chocolate is associated with a reduced risk of stroke, but clinical trial evidence is more nuanced.

### Summary of Evidence
* **Observational & Genetic Data:** Meta-analyses of prospective population studies show an inverse relationship between moderate chocolate intake and stroke risk (https://heart.bmj.com/content/105/1/49). A Mendelian randomization study indicated a causal link between dark chocolate intake and reduced risk of essential hypertension, a major stroke risk factor (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-50351-6).
* **Biological Mechanisms:** Cocoa is rich in flavanols (such as epicatechin), which increase nitric oxide production, improve blood vessel dilation, lower blood pressure, and inhibit platelet aggregation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022066/).
* **Randomized Clinical Trials:** The COSMOS trial tested daily cocoa flavanol extract (500 mg) in over 21,000 older adults. While supplementation reduced cardiovascular mortality by 27%, it did not achieve a statistically significant reduction in overall stroke incidence (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(22)00275-1/fulltext).

### Important Considerations
Commercial dark chocolate products vary widely in flavanol concentration because conventional processing destroys these compounds. Additionally, sugar, saturated fat, and calories in standard dark chocolate bars can counteract vascular benefits if consumed in excess. Isolated cocoa flavanol extracts provide these compounds without extra calories.
